blocks.title: Ideal and real fluids
blocks.text: An ideal fluid is a fluid that does not have viscosity and cannot be compressed; this type of fluid cannot exist practically. All types of fluids that possess viscosity are classified as real fluids, for example kerosene, castor oil and honey.
Comparison of ideal and real fluids

An example of an ideal fluid cannot be provided, because it does not exist in the real world but only in theory. Every fluid we see around us, like water, diesel, petrol and honey, is a real fluid. Differences in viscosity are found in real life, for example honey is more viscous than water. Bernoulli's equation states that the speed of fluid flow is increased as a result of a simultaneous decrease in the potential energy of the fluid or a decrease in the static pressure on the fluid. When a fluid is viscous, it essentially refers to the thickness of the fluid or the friction the fluid faces while flowing. Therefore ideal fluids do not face the opposing force and have a non-viscous flow, while real fluids have a viscous flow.

items: Ideal fluids are incompressible: neither the density nor the volume of the fluid changes with pressure, whereas real fluids are very much compressible.

Bulk modulus depends inversely on the volume change; the volume change for ideal fluids is zero, so the bulk modulus is infinite for ideal fluids. Real fluids are subject to volume change and therefore have a finite bulk modulus.
As ideal fluids exist only in theory they are not subject to surface tension; for real fluids surface tension becomes applicable.

blocks.text: In simpler words, ideal fluids are imaginary in nature, which means they do not exist in nature, whereas real fluids very much exist. Ideal fluids do not have any viscosity, or can be said to have zero viscosity; real fluids have viscosity.

blocks.prompt: What is the difference between a real fluid, an ideal fluid and a superfluid, and which of them really exists (constructed response 5.5)?
blocks.explanation: An ideal fluid has no viscosity, is incompressible and has no surface tension; it exists only in theory. A real fluid has viscosity, some compressibility and surface tension, and is every ordinary fluid. A superfluid is a real substance, such as helium-4 below about 2 K, that actually has zero viscosity; real fluids and superfluids exist, ideal fluids do not.

items: Ideal fluid: no viscosity, incompressible (infinite bulk modulus), no surface tension, theory only. Real fluid: viscous (honey more than water), compressible, finite bulk modulus, surface tension: water, diesel, petrol, honey, kerosene, castor oil.
